notes: 100% pass rate with the skill vs 45.8% baseline, consistent across all 3 topics (tech-confession, personal-development-confession, church-drama) -- not driven by one easy case.

The single most discriminating assertion across all evals: question-style H2 headers. With-skill hit this in 3/3 runs; baseline hit it in 0/3 -- baseline defaulted to zero section breaks every time, writing continuous single-block essays instead.

Baseline drifted into an invented fact once (a '$20 a month' Claude Pro price never given in eval 1's prompt) -- a real hallucination risk the skill's 'get the real story first, don't invent facts' step is designed to prevent, and did prevent in all 3 with-skill runs.

Baseline endings leaned on exactly the constructions no-ai-slop's own pattern list flags as generic AI tells: an 'isn't X, it's Y' binary contrast (eval 2) and interpretive metadiscourse narrating 'there's something fitting about that whole arc' (eval 3) -- the with-skill runs avoided both by using genuine callbacks instead.

Time and token cost: with-skill runs took ~2.9x longer (222s vs 76s mean) and used ~1.6x the tokens (70.6k vs 45.4k mean), almost entirely the cost of reading voice-examples.md and running the no-ai-slop pass. Worth knowing as a cost/quality tradeoff, though absolute times are still well under 5 minutes.

Eval 2's with-skill run flagged its own judgment call for review: it kept a 'not X, it's Y' binary-contrast line ('A retreat isn't a sustainable state. It's a moment.') because voice-examples.md shows Asher using that exact shape since 2018 -- this pattern isn't in the skill's current explicit override list and may be worth adding.

Assertion critique: 'does not contain banned buzzwords' passed 6/6 across both configurations and never discriminated -- neither model reaches for corporate buzzwords unprompted at this task size, so it's a weak assertion here (still worth keeping as a regression guard, just don't read much into it passing).

Only one grading judgment worth flagging as borderline: eval 1's with-skill ending ('Funny how the discipline and the mistake can look exactly the same from the inside') was scored as a genuine callback since it reuses 'cold turkey' from three paragraphs earlier, but it's also a fairly aphoristic closing line -- a stricter grader might call this closer to a kicker than a callback. Human review of that one line is the most useful single thing to check.
